title: Yellow Hickory Leaves with Daisy
altText: A close-up painting of five large, vivid yellow hickory leaves with a white daisy in the lower middle, set against a white background.

source.verifiedBy: Art Institute of Chicago API record: title, artist (Georgia O'Keeffe, American, 1887-1986), date, medium, place of origin, credit line, thumbnail alt text (a close-up view of five hickory leaves in vivid yellow, a white daisy in the lower middle portion, on a white background), curatorial description (greatly enlarged scale; foliage seen on summer walks near Lake George, New York; realistic handling and close focus give an abstract quality) and public-domain flag (false) read from the record. context: Painted in 1928 by Georgia O'Keeffe. The museum says she painted hickory leaves and a white daisy at a greatly enlarged scale, drawing on foliage she saw on summer walks near Lake George, New York, and that she hoped monumental subjects would prompt viewers to look at nature in a fresh way.

descriptions.k: Giant leaves! Five bright yellow leaves and one white daisy fill the picture. The background is white. They are painted close up and very big. Which leaf is your favorite?
descriptions.g12: Georgia O'Keeffe painted five yellow hickory leaves and a white daisy, very big and very close. It is like looking at them through a magnifying glass. The background is white. What do you notice about the shapes of the leaves? How do the yellow and white look together?
descriptions.g35: Georgia O'Keeffe painted Yellow Hickory Leaves with Daisy in 1928, showing five yellow leaves and a white daisy greatly enlarged. She was inspired by plants on summer walks near Lake George, New York. The leaves are painted so close up that they seem almost abstract. Why might she make small plants look so big? What new details do you notice?
descriptions.g68: O'Keeffe enlarged hickory leaves and a daisy to monumental size, based on foliage she saw on walks near Lake George, New York. The museum says her realistic handling combined with the close focus gives the painting an abstract quality, and that she hoped enlarged subjects would make viewers see nature in a fresh way. How does magnification change how you look, and what do you notice that you would miss in a small plant?
descriptions.g910: In Yellow Hickory Leaves with Daisy (1928), O'Keeffe magnifies leaves and a white daisy against a white ground. The museum notes the abstract quality created by realistic handling and a close focus, and her hope that monumental subjects would make viewers look at nature anew. Consider how scale, cropping, and color isolate simple forms into near-abstraction, and how that strategy changes the viewer's attention.
descriptions.g1112: O'Keeffe's 1928 painting turns a small piece of nature into a monumental image: enlarged yellow leaves and a white daisy on a white ground. The museum describes how realistic handling and tight focus give the work an abstract quality, and notes her intention to prompt fresh looking. How does magnification reframe the botanical subject, and how does the painting negotiate between close observation and abstraction in American modernism?

k.light: Where does the picture look the brightest?
k.meaning: Why might an artist paint a plant so big?
k.culture: Where have you seen leaves change color?
k.technique: How would you paint a very big leaf?
k.personal: Which plant would you paint very big?

teacherNote.context: A 1928 oil painting by Georgia O'Keeffe in the Art Institute of Chicago showing greatly enlarged yellow hickory leaves and a white daisy. The museum links the subject to walks near Lake George, New York. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Have students use a magnifier on a leaf, then draw one part very large.
Ask students to compare a small sketch of a leaf with a full-page enlargement.
Discuss how making something big can change how we see it.
